title: Initial-form minimality for maximal projective-order forms
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $r\geq0$, and $B=k[X_0,\ldots,X_r]$ with all variables of degree one [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. Let $\mathfrak p\subset k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$ be a prime ideal, put $L=k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]_{\mathfrak p}$ and $N=\mathfrak pL$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], and define $\delta_d:B_d\to L$ by $\delta_d(\phi)=\phi(1,t_1,\ldots,t_r)/1$. Put $U_d=\{\phi\in B_d:\delta_d(\phi)\in N^d\}$. For $h\in L$ its order is $\sup\{n:h\in N^n\}$; for finite order $n$, its initial form is its class in $N^n/N^{n+1}\subset\operatorname{gr}_NL$ [def-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring]. Let $b\geq0$ and let nonzero forms $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_b$ of degrees $1\leq e_1\leq\cdots\leq e_b$ belong to $U_{e_i}$. Suppose they minimally generate their homogeneous ideal in $B$, meaning that no $\phi_i$ belongs to the ideal generated by the other forms. Then $\operatorname{ord}_N\delta_{e_i}(\phi_i)=e_i$ for each $i$, and their initial forms minimally generate the homogeneous ideal they generate in $\operatorname{gr}_NL$. The assertion includes the empty family.

source.place: Hironaka, Certain numerical characters of singularities (1970), Lemma 15, pp.170–171. Read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED. ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only; no Stacks tag states this assertion.

proof.text: Put $K=L/N=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and let $a_i\in K$ be the residue of $t_i/1$, using [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. The map $k\to K$ is injective: the kernel of a unital map from a field to a nonzero field is zero. Let $P=K[Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]$, $I=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_r)$, $S=P_I$ and $M=IS$. The substitution $t_i\mapsto a_i+Z_i$ induces a local map $\tau:L\to S$. Indeed, for $s\notin\mathfrak p$ its residue $s(a)$ is nonzero, so $s(a+Z)$ is invertible in $S$, and explicitly $\tau(f/s)=f(a+Z)/s(a+Z)$. For $f\in\mathfrak p$, $f(a+Z)$ has constant coefficient zero and hence lies in $I$. Thus $\tau(N)\subseteq M$ and $\tau(N^n)\subseteq M^n$ for every $n$. No maximality or separability assumption on $\mathfrak p$ is used.

Agent adaptation: use the residue-field diagonal point instead of an algebraically closed extension. ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: Let $B_K=K[X_0,\ldots,X_r]$, and denote the coefficient images of the given forms by $\phi_i^K$. Identify $B\otimes_k K$ with $B_K$ by $X^\alpha\otimes c\mapsto cX^\alpha$; the inverse sends $\sum c_\alpha X^\alpha$ to $\sum X^\alpha\otimes c_\alpha$. Multiplying monomials checks these are inverse algebra maps. By [lem-weil-pbc-field-extension-base-change-faithfully-flat] and [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ideal-contraction], $B\to B_K$ is injective and contracts the extended ideal generated by any subfamily to that subfamily's ideal in $B$. Consequently all $\phi_i^K$ are nonzero and no one belongs to the ideal of the others: such membership would contract to the prohibited membership in $B$. Coefficient extension preserves the degrees because it preserves each monomial and its nonzero coefficient.

source.place: Tags 00HP (lemma-ff), 00HI (lemma-flat-base-change), 05CK (lemma-faithfully-flat-universally-injective), applied to coefficient extension; Hironaka Lemma 15, pp.170–171, SB under coefficient extensions.

proof.text: Here is the elementary coefficient calculation in $S$. For $f\in P$, $f/1\in M^n$ if and only if all its terms have degree at least $n$. To see the forward implication, express $f/1$ as a finite sum $\sum_{|\alpha|=n}(u_\alpha/s_\alpha)Z^\alpha$, allowing zero coefficients. The product $s=\prod_\alpha s_\alpha$ has $s(0)\ne0$ and $sf\in I^n$; equality after localization gives this polynomial equality since a polynomial ring over a field is a domain (the leading term of a product is the product of leading terms). If the least nonzero homogeneous component of $f$ had degree $d<n$, that of $sf$ would be $s(0)f_d\ne0$, a contradiction. Conversely every monomial of degree at least $n$ is divisible by a degree-$n$ monomial. This also proves the explicit graded isomorphism $\beta:K[Z]\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{gr}_M S$, $Z_i\mapsto[Z_i]_1$. It is injective on degree $n$ by the coefficient test. It is surjective there because a fraction $f/s\in M^n$ has $f\in I^n$ and its class is $s(0)^{-1}f_n$: the remainder has numerator in $I^{n+1}$. Products of representatives give multiplicativity. The degree-zero map is the identity of $K$.

source.place: Hironaka, Certain numerical characters of singularities (1970), Lemma 15, printed pp.170–171, read online at https://scispace.com/pdf/certain-numerical-characters-of-singularities-18d51ii5bz.pdf; archival copy WANTED. Agent adaptation: use the residue-field diagonal point instead of an algebraically closed extension. ILO VIII 2.3.13 is ancestor motivation only.

proof.text: For each $i$ define $F_i(X_0,Z)=\phi_i^K(X_0,a_1X_0+Z_1,\ldots,a_rX_0+Z_r)$. This is a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree $e_i$: the substitution is linear and has inverse $Z_j=X_j-a_jX_0$. Write it uniquely as $\sum_{|\alpha|\le e_i}c_{i\alpha}X_0^{e_i-|\alpha|}Z^\alpha$. Its specialization $q_i(Z)=F_i(1,Z)=\phi_i^K(1,a+Z)$ is nonzero, because distinct $\alpha$ in that expression remain distinct after specialization. Moreover $q_i/1=\tau(\delta_{e_i}(\phi_i))\in M^{e_i}$. By step 3 all $c_{i\alpha}$ with $|\alpha|<e_i$ vanish. Thus $F_i=q_i(Z)$ is independent of $X_0$, and $q_i$ is nonzero homogeneous of degree exactly $e_i$. Step 3 gives $q_i/1\notin M^{e_i+1}$.

proof.text: Write $h_i=\delta_{e_i}(\phi_i)$. It belongs to $N^{e_i}$ by assumption. It cannot belong to $N^{e_i+1}$, since step 1 would imply $q_i/1=\tau(h_i)\in M^{e_i+1}$, contrary to step 4. Hence $\operatorname{ord}_N h_i=e_i$. On homogeneous classes define $\gamma:\operatorname{gr}_N L\to\operatorname{gr}_M S$ by $[h]_n\mapsto[\tau(h)]_n$. This is well defined because $\tau(N^{n+1})\subseteq M^{n+1}$, and preserves sums, products and the unit by the representative formulas of [def-weil-pbc-associated-graded-ring]. Its degree-zero map $L/N\to S/M$ is the identity of $K$, and for $\eta_i=\operatorname{in}_N h_i$ one has $\gamma(\eta_i)=\beta(q_i)$. We need no injectivity assertion about $\gamma$.

proof.text: The invertible linear substitution of step 4 takes $\phi_i^K$ to $q_i$ in $K[X_0,Z]$. Thus step 2 implies that no $q_i$ belongs to the ideal of the other $q_j$ in that ring, and hence none does in its subring $K[Z]$: a relation in the subring would also hold in the larger ring. If some $\eta_i$ belonged to the ideal generated by the other initial forms in $\operatorname{gr}_N L$, apply the ring map $\gamma$ of step 5, then the inverse of $\beta$ from step 3. The resulting equality would put $q_i$ in the ideal of the other $q_j$ in $K[Z]$, a contradiction. Therefore the $\eta_i$ minimally generate their ideal. That ideal is homogeneous: in any finite sum of their graded-ring multiples, the component of a specified degree is the sum of the corresponding homogeneous components of the multiples times $\eta_i$. This proves every clause. If $b=0$, both families are empty and generate the zero ideal. If $r=0$, then $K[Z]=K$ has no nonzero positive-degree homogeneous polynomials, so step 4 rules out a nonempty family; the empty case still applies.
